profile.name: Yashvardhan Singh
profile.bio:
I'm Yashvardhan Singh, a digital integrated circuit design engineer.

I work on hardware acceleration, digital ASIC design, open-source silicon, machine learning for EDA, and post-CMOS devices like spintronics (CMOS-MTJ). I like taking designs all the way from RTL to GDSII. I also co-founded [ChipMIT](#volunteering), India's first student-run chip design club.
profile.before: At 16, I started a esports team, grew it to a 2,000+ member community, ran a 64-team national tournament, and later saw it merge into a larger organization. I also did freelance graphic design for four years ([portfolio](https://www.behance.net/zmagnus)). Both still help when I'm running events or doing presentations.

news.text: Visited SEMICON India 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, with my team from ST.

Our ASCON-128a crypto accelerator got tapeout approval at the IEEE SSCS PICO Chipathon 2026. We couldn't make the final wafer run because of export rules on encryption hardware. A paper on it is under review at IEEE ICEE 2026.
Started a year-long internship at STMicroelectronics, in the MDRF group in Greater Noida.
My first-author paper on sense amplifiers for CMOS-MTJ compute-in-memory is out in [IEEE JXCDC](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11506373).
Handed over as President of ChipMIT and joined its Advisory Board.
Led Silizium 2026, ChipMIT's 3-day semiconductor summit with talks from Intel and AMD, an academic panel, and three hands-on workshops.
Presented ChipMIT's work to Karthik Anand, AVP at Marvell Technology.
Attended VLSID 2026 in Pune on a Local Fellowship.
Our team won the Edge AI Accelerator track at Silicon Sprint 2025 (IEEE NITK, IEEE RVCE, Tenstorrent) by building a 4×4 systolic array in 24 hours.
Project Kalki got a Special Mention at SYNCHRON'25 and 2nd place at the BIS ECE case study competition.
Posted two preprints: one on spintronic cryptography (SSRN) and one on dopants in NC junctionless FinFET sensors (Research Square).
ChipMIT ran Semiconductor Showdown, MIT Manipal's first chip design contest, with Marvell and the ECE department. 150+ people took part.
Finished the Samsung Fellowship (ISWDP Cohort 5) by IISc, Synopsys and Samsung, including the advanced Sentaurus TCAD track.
Became Entrepreneur in Residence at Ecosight Technologies (BeePrecise).
Joined BeePrecise in Bangalore as a hardware intern.
Put my 32-bit Brent-Kung adder study on [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18070).
Co-founded ChipMIT with Megh Giri.
Won Best Hack at M# Manipal Hackathon 2024, out of 408 teams.
Started teaching maths to Grade 6 students in Pune with Teach For India.
Summer research internship on spintronics at IIT (BHU) Varanasi.

notes.title: Start here
notes.body:
These are my working notes on chip design, written the way I'd explain things to a friend. They're not polished, and they change as I learn.

Notes link to each other, like [[Setup and hold time]] or [[Clock domain crossing]]. The graph shows how everything connects: click any dot to open that note.

If something here looks wrong, I'd love to hear about it.

notes.title: Setup and hold time
notes.body:
Every flip-flop needs its input **D** to sit still for a short time around the clock edge.

- **Setup time** ($t_{su}$): how long D must be stable *before* the edge.
- **Hold time** ($t_h$): how long D must stay stable *after* the edge.

Break either one and the flop can go metastable, which is also the core problem in [[Clock domain crossing]].

## Setup check

Data launched on one clock edge must arrive before the next edge, with setup time to spare:

$$t_{cq} + t_{logic,max} + t_{su} \le T_{clk} + t_{skew}$$

If this fails, you can slow the clock, shorten the logic path, or split it with a pipeline stage.

## Hold check

New data must not arrive *too early* and overwrite the value being captured on the same edge:

$$t_{cq} + t_{logic,min} \ge t_h + t_{skew}$$

Hold does not depend on the clock period, so slowing the clock never fixes a hold violation. The usual fix is adding delay (buffers) on the short path.

> Here $t_{skew}$ = capture clock arrival time minus launch clock arrival time.

notes.title: Clock domain crossing
notes.body: A clock domain crossing (CDC) happens when a signal made on one clock is read by flops on a different, unrelated clock. The two clocks' edges have no fixed relationship, so sometimes the receiving flop samples the signal right while it changes. That breaks [[Setup and hold time]] and the flop goes **metastable**.

notes.title: Systolic arrays
notes.body:
A systolic array is a grid of small, identical processing elements (PEs). Each PE does a multiply-accumulate (MAC) and passes data to its neighbours every clock cycle, like a heartbeat pumping data through the grid. That's where the name comes from. The original roots stem from H T Kung's paper on Systolics, who is the same person who was involved in Brent-Kung adders.

I built a 4×4 one in [Project Kalki](./#projects).
